stances.claim: Congress should convene, discuss, and vote separately in all three acts of constituent-assembly proceedings -- joint sitting is not constitutionally required for amendment.

Art. XVII, Sec. 1 says only 'three-fourths of all its Members' without textual joint-sitting requirement; unlike the war-declaration, canvassing, and VP-vacancy provisions, the Constitution does not say so 'expressly and in unmistakable language.'
What is not expressly or impliedly prohibited by the Constitution may be done by Congress within its powers -- separate convening and deliberating is not prohibited and is within congressional power.
Separate voting can be implied from the bicameral nature of Congress: if it votes separately in legislation, it must vote separately in its constituent function.

Justice Azcuna's framer-view that conversion to con-ass is incomplete until adoption-and-passage by the necessary votes is satisfied by RBH No. 2's express 'each House voting separately' language; the very act of separately assembling and deliberating is itself proof of conversion ('actions speak louder than words').
Such proceedings would, in CJ's humble opinion, hurdle a Supreme Court challenge; both Houses should also approve 'Internal Rules of the Constituent Assembly' integrating the 'separate' concept.

one_paragraph_summary: On the procedural question of how Congress should act as a constituent assembly (con-ass) to amend the Constitution, Panganiban gives a thesis-first answer: 'separately' in all three acts -- convening, deliberating, and voting. The House Committee on Constitutional Amendments, having voted 64-3-3 on Resolution of Both Houses No. 2 (sponsored by Speaker Velasco), agreed; the resolution amends the nationalistic provisions of Articles XII, XIV, and XVI by inserting 'unless otherwise provided by law' (private land ownership remains in Filipino hands). Respectfully disagreeing with his 'esteemed friend' retired Justice Vicente V. Mendoza -- who reads the Constitution to require joint deliberation with separate voting -- CJ argues that Art. XVII, Sec. 1 mentions only 'three-fourths of all its Members,' without a joint-sitting requirement. The Constitution speaks expressly and in unmistakable language when it does require joint sitting (declaration of war, canvassing the presidential vote, confirming a VP nominee), and is silent here. By the well-settled rule, what is not expressly or impliedly prohibited may be done by Congress; separate voting is also implied from bicameralism (if Congress votes separately in legislation, so must it in its constituent function). Echoing retired Justice Adolfo Azcuna, a framer of the 1987 Constitution, on the timing of con-ass conversion, CJ argues that the RBH's express 'each House voting separately' text plus the very conduct of separately assembling are more than enough proof -- 'actions speak louder than words.' Such proceedings would, in his humble opinion, hurdle a Supreme Court challenge; he recommends that both Houses also adopt 'Internal Rules of the Constituent Assembly' integrating the 'separate' concept.
